marble.name: Radiometric Dating
marble.subject: Science
marble.description: Explain how radiometric dating works — radioactive isotopes decay at a known rate (half-life), so measuring the ratio of parent to daughter isotope in a rock or fossil gives an absolute age; distinguish between carbon-14 (useful up to ~50,000 years) and uranium-lead (useful for millions to billions of years)
marble.prompt: If you was told a dinosaur bone was dated using uranium-lead radiometric dating, could they explain what that means — what is decaying, why the rate of decay is useful, and roughly why scientists don't use carbon-14 for 70-million-year-old bones?

cluster.summary: Your child is exploring the fascinating world of dinosaurs — learning about different species, understanding what fossils tell us about these ancient creatures, and discovering how scientists study life from long ago.

misconceptions: 'You can carbon-date dinosaur bones' — C-14's ~50,000-year range is far too short for 66-million-year fossils.
'Radiometric dating counts down from when the animal died like a stopwatch' — it reads the parent:daughter ratio of a decay process.
'After two half-lives everything has decayed' — a quarter of the parent remains; decay is exponential, never reaching zero cleanly.
'We date the fossil itself' — usually the surrounding volcanic rock is dated, bracketing the fossil's age.
'Half-life changes with conditions' — it is essentially constant, which is what makes it a reliable clock.

authoredAnswer: No. Carbon-14 has a short half-life and is only useful up to roughly 50,000 years, but non-avian dinosaurs are around 66+ million years old — any carbon-14 would have decayed away long ago. Dinosaur-age rock is dated with long-lived isotopes like uranium-lead or potassium-argon. wrongAnswers.wrong: Yes — carbon dating works on anything old, including dinosaur bones.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Applies carbon-14 to million-year-old material without noticing its time limit.
wrongAnswers.fix: Introduce half-life ranges: carbon-14 (~50,000 yr max) versus uranium-lead (millions to billions of years); match the clock to the age.

wrongAnswers.wrong: You just measure how long the clock inside the bone has been ticking.
wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Describes dating as counting time directly rather than measuring a parent:daughter ratio.
wrongAnswers.fix: Recast it as a ratio measurement: the proportion of parent left versus daughter formed, read against the known half-life.

wrongAnswers.revealedBy: Says all the parent is gone after one half-life, or treats decay as linear.
wrongAnswers.fix: Model repeated halving — half remains after one half-life, a quarter after two — not complete or linear decay.
